DETAILED ACTION
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Claim Interpretation
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f):
(f) Element in Claim for a Combination. – An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph:
An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
The claims in this application are given their broadest reasonable interpretation using the plain meaning of the claim language in light of the specification as it would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.  The broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim element (also commonly referred to as a claim limitation) is limited by the description in the specification when 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, is invoked.
As explained in MPEP § 2181, subsection I, claim limitations that meet the following three-prong test will be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph:
(A)	the claim limitation uses the term “means” or “step” or a term used as a substitute for “means” that is a generic placeholder (also called a nonce term or a non-structural term having no specific structural meaning) for performing the claimed function;
(B)	the term “means” or “step” or the generic placeholder is modified by functional language, typically, but not always linked by the transition word “for” (e.g., “means for”) or another linking word or phrase, such as “configured to” or “so that”; and
(C)	the term “means” or “step” or the generic placeholder is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
Use of the word “means” (or “step”) in a claim with functional language creates a rebuttable presumption that the claim limitation is to be treated in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph. The presumption that the claim limitation is interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, is rebutted when the claim limitation recites sufficient structure, material, or acts to entirely perform the recited function.
Absence of the word “means” (or “step”) in a claim creates a rebuttable presumption that the claim limitation is not to be treated in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph. The presumption that the claim limitation is not interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, is rebutted when the claim limitation recites function without reciting sufficient structure, material or acts to entirely perform the recited function.
Claim limitations in this application that use the word “means” (or “step”) are being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, except as otherwise indicated in an Office action. Conversely, claim limitations in this application that do not use the word “means” (or “step”) are not being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, except as otherwise indicated in an Office action.
This application includes one or more claim limitations that do not use the word “means,” but are nonetheless being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, because the claim limitation(s) uses a generic placeholder that is coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure to perform the recited function and the generic placeholder is not preceded by a structural modifier.  Such claim limitation(s) is/are: “communication module” in claims 1, 17, 31, and 45, and “remote processing device” in claims 17 and 45.
Because this/these claim limitation(s) is/are being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, it/they is/are being interpreted to cover the corresponding structure described in the specification as performing the claimed function, and equivalents thereof. Specifically, the communication module is being interpreted to cover a memory and processor (see [0045]) and equivalents thereof; the remote processing device is being interpreted to cover either a cloud-based server (see [0045]), or may be included within the communication module (see [0046]) and equivalents thereof.
If applicant does not intend to have this/these limitation(s) interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, applicant may:  (1) amend the claim limitation(s) to avoid it/them being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph (e.g., by reciting sufficient structure to perform the claimed function); or (2) present a sufficient showing that the claim limitation(s) recite(s) sufficient structure to perform the claimed function so as to avoid it/them being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 101
35 U.S.C. 101 reads as follows:
Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
Claims 1-3, 5-10, 17-19, 21-26, 31, and 45 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception, specifically an abstract idea (mathematical calculations and/or mental processes of transforming and demixing signals) without significantly more.
Step 1
Regarding claims 1-3, 5-10, 17-19, 21-26, 31, and 45, the claimed invention is directed to statutory subject matter.
Step 2A, Prong One
Regarding independent claims 1, 17, 31, and 45, the recited steps are directed to mathematical calculations and/or mental processes of performing concepts by a human (see MPEP 2106.04(a)(2) subsections (I) and (III)).
The limitations of “transform/transforming, in response to a change in the force data indicative of a change in a load on the article and based on a determination of a plurality of physiological sources on the article, the force data from each of the plurality of sensors into a corresponding plurality of physiological signals,” “determine/determining, based on the plurality of physiological signals, a source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources,” “separating into components each of the plurality of physiological signals, wherein the components correspond to each of the plurality of physiological sources at each of the plurality of sensors,” and “compositing the separated components for each of the plurality of physiological sources, wherein the compositing forms the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources” are processes, as drafted, that cover mathematical calculations and/or performance of the limitation by a human.
The computations are simple enough to be practically performed in the human mind or through critical thinking. Note that even if most humans would use a physical aid (e.g., pen and paper, a slide rule, or a calculator) to help them complete the recited steps, the use of such physical aid does not negate the mental nature of this limitation. Nor does the recitation of a processor in the claim negate the mental nature of this limitation because the claim here merely uses the processor as a tool to perform the otherwise mental process.
Step 2A, Prong Two
For independent claims 1, 17, 31, and 45, the judicial exception is not integrated into a practical application. In particular, the claims recite the additional elements of “a communication module…,” “at least one data processor…,” “at least one memory…,” and “a remote processing device…” These elements are recited at a high-level of generality and amount to nothing more than parts of a generic computer. Merely including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer does not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application. The claims further recite “a plurality of sensors…each of the plurality of sensors configured/is configured to engage with (a member of) an article on which a first user is positioned…each of the plurality of sensors configured/is configured to measure force.” This limitation amounts to nothing more than mere pre-solution activity of data-gathering.
Step 2B
The claims do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. As discussed above with respect to integration of the abstract idea into a practical application, the additional element of sensing force using a plurality of sensors engaged with member(s) of an article on which a user is positioned amounts to no more than mere pre-solution activity of data gathering, which does not amount to an inventive concept. Additionally, using force sensors attached to an article on which a user is positioned is well-understood in the art. For example, in the review article “Ballistocardiography and Seismocardiography: A Review of Recent Advances” by Inan et al., the authors indicate that load cells (i.e., sensors configured to measure force) attached to legs of beds (“configured to engage with a member of an article on which a first user is positioned”) for the purpose of ballistocardiography is known in the art (see section titled “Bed-Based BCG Systems” on pg. 4).
Regarding dependent claims 2-3, 5-10, 18-19, and 21-26, the limitations further define the limitations already indicated as being directed to an abstract idea.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
(a)(2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b), in which the patent or application, as the case may be, names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claims 1-3, 17-19, 31, and 45 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by US Patent Application Publication US-2020/0110194-A1 to Young et al. (hereinafter “Young”).

each of the plurality of sensors configured to engage with an article on which a first user is positioned (Fig. 1 shows the plurality of sensors engaged with a bed (i.e., an article) on which a user is positioned)
and each of the plurality of sensors configured to measure force ( [0063] states that the sensors may be force sensors and [0030] states that the sensors detect (measure) force)
a communication module in communication with each of the plurality of sensors (e.g.,  the portion of controller 200 that collects signals from sensors 106 described in [0036])
wherein the communication module receives force data transmitted from each of the plurality of sensors ([0036] states that the communication module collects signals from sensors 106, which are configured to measure force)
and an apparatus (Fig. 2 and [0037], e.g., controller 200, cloud based computer 212, and/or off-site controller 214) comprising:
at least one data processor (Fig. 2 and [0037], e.g., the processing components of controller 200, cloud based computer 212, and/or off-site controller 214)
and at least one memory (the instructions for the processing performed by the at least one processor would necessarily be stored on a memory) storing instructions which, when executed by the at least one data processor, cause the apparatus to at least: receive, from the communication module, the force data ([0036-37] indicate that the apparatus receives force data from the communication module)
transform, in response to a change in the force data indicative of a change in a load on the article ([0053] states that load (force) data can be used to determine presence of a subject on a substrate (indicative of a change in a load on the article); [0053] further states that the system can wake up in response to detecting the presence of a subject on the article)
and based on a determination of a plurality of physiological sources on the article ([0034] states that the system can differentiate between two or more bodies (plurality of physiological sources) on the bed (article)),
[transform] the force data from each of the plurality of sensors into a corresponding plurality of physiological signals (micro signals from the load sensors (force data from each of the plurality of sensors) are processed (transformed) to determine a variety of data, such as cardiac and respiratory signals (plurality of physiological signals), see [0042]-[0043])
and determine, based on the plurality of physiological signals, a source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources ([0034] states that the system can determine cardiac and respiratory signals for multiple people (each of the plurality of physiological sources))
wherein the determination of the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources comprises: separating into components each of the plurality of physiological signals wherein the components correspond to each of the plurality of physiological sources at each of the plurality of sensors ([0047]; during superposition analysis, the contribution of each individual source (components of each of the plurality of physiological signals at each of the plurality of sensors) is determined)
and compositing the separated components for each of the plurality of physiological sources, wherein the compositing forms the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources ([0047]; the resultant responses are added to determine the “true result” (the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources)).
Regarding claim 2, Young discloses the system of claim 1, wherein the determination of the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources is based on a model for each of the plurality of physiological sources wherein each model comprises the components, the components defining a contribution of a respective physiological source to each of the plurality of physiological sources (the superposition analysis described in [0047] is considered a model for each of the plurality of physiological sources under its broadest reasonable interpretation).
Regarding claim 3, Young discloses the system of claim 1, wherein, based on the determination of the plurality of physiological sources on the article, the physiological signals are based on the force data from at least two of the plurality of sensors (the use of multiple (i.e., at least 2) sensors is necessary to determine cardiac and respiratory signals for multiple people (see [0034]), therefore at least two sensors would be used in the superposition analysis described in [0047]).

compositing the separated components for each of the plurality of physiological sources, wherein the compositing forms the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources ([0047]; the resultant responses are added to determine the “true result” (the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources)).
Regarding claim 18, Young teaches the method of claim 17, wherein the determination of the source physiological signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources is based on a model for each of the plurality of physiological sources, wherein each model comprises the components, the components defining a contribution of a respective physiological source to each of the plurality of physiological sources (the superposition analysis described in [0047] is considered a model for each of the plurality of physiological sources under its broadest reasonable interpretation).

Regarding claim 31, Young teaches an apparatus (e.g., the apparatus of Fig. 2, including controller 200, cloud based computer 212, and/or off-site controller 214), comprising:
at least one data processor (Fig. 2 and [0037], e.g., the processing components of controller 200, cloud based computer 212, and/or off-site controller 214); and at least one memory (the instructions for the processing performed by the at least one processor would necessarily be stored on a memory) storing instructions which, when executed by the at least one data processor, cause the apparatus to at least: receive, from a communication module (e.g.,  the portion of controller 200 that collects signals from sensors 106 described in [0036]) in communication with a plurality of sensors (Fig. 2 shows a plurality of sensors 106), force data ([0036-37] indicate that the apparatus receives force data from the communication module), wherein each of the plurality of sensors is configured to engage with a member of an article on which a first user is positioned (Fig. 1 shows the plurality of sensors engaged with a bed, i.e., an article, on which a user is positioned), and further

Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary.  Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.
Claims 5-8 and 21-24 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Young in view of US Patent Application Publication US-2005/0124864-A1 to Mack et al. (hereinafter “Mack”).
Regarding claims 5 and 21, Young discloses the system of claim 1 and the method of claim 17. Although Young discloses time-domain and/or frequency-domain filtering the force data to obtain a plurality of respiratory signals corresponding to each of the plurality of sensors, that feature does not appear to be explicitly supported by the provisional application (‘613 to which Young claims domestic benefit).
However, Mack teaches a system that transforms force data (input signal 705) into respiratory signals (chest movement output signal 740) using frequency-domain filtering (2nd order band pass filter 725); see [0063] and Fig. 7. Paragraph [0033] states that the vibration sensors, which sense input signal 705, may use load cells, which measure force data.
Mack is considered to be analogous to the claimed invention because they are both within the same field of non-invasive monitoring of physiological signals using sensors attached to articles on which a user is positioned. Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified Young by incorporating the teachings of Mack by utilizing frequency-domain filtering to transform the force data into respiratory signals and to do this for each of the plurality of sensors. Doing so would allow the system to separate respiratory and cardiac output signals from the force data (see Mack [0063]).
Regarding claims 6 and 22, Young in view of Mack discloses the system of claim 5 and the method of claim 21, wherein a source respiratory signal is determined, based on the plurality of respiratory signals, for each of the plurality of physiological sources (Young [0034] states that respiratory signals (a source respiratory signal) are determined for multiple people (i.e., each of the plurality of physiological sources)), and wherein the execution of the instructions further cause the apparatus to at least/the method further comprises: identify/identifying, from the source respiratory signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources, one or more respiratory parameters (Young [0034] states that respiration rate and respiration condition (one or more respiratory parameters) can be determined from the source respiratory signals).
Regarding claims 7 and 23, Young discloses the system of claim 1 and the method of claim 17. Although Young discloses time-domain and/or frequency-domain filtering the force data to obtain a plurality of ballistocardiogram signals corresponding to each of the plurality of sensors, that feature does not appear to be explicitly supported by the provisional application.
However, Mack teaches a system that transforms force data (input signal 705) into ballistocardiogram signals (cardiac output signal 765) using frequency-domain filtering (2nd order low pass filter 745 and/or 3rd order high pass filter 750), see [0064] and Fig. 7. Paragraph [0033] states that the vibration sensors, which sense input signal 705, may use load cells, which measure force data. Mack [0006]  states that ballistocardiography is the study of the cardiac system by measuring forces related to the contraction and relaxation of the heart... The cardiac output signal 765 is considered to be a ballistocardiogram signal because it was created by measuring forces related to heart activity using the vibration sensors.
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified Young by incorporating the teachings of Mack to utilize frequency-domain filtering to transform the force data into ballistocardiogram signals and to do this for each of the plurality of sensors. Doing so would allow the system to separate respiratory and cardiac output signals from the force data (see Mack [0063]).
Regarding claims 8 and 24, Young in view of Mack discloses the system of claim 7 and the method of claim 23, wherein a source ballistocardiogram signal is determined, based on the plurality of ballistocardiogram signals, for each of the plurality of physiological sources (Young [0034] states that cardiac signals (source ballistocardiogram signal) are determined for multiple people (i.e., each of the plurality of physiological sources)), and wherein the execution of the instructions further cause the apparatus to at least/the method further comprises: identify/identifying, from the source ballistocardiogram signal for each of the plurality of physiological sources, one or more ballistocardiogram parameters (Young [0034] states that heart rate, heart condition, and beat to beat variation (one or more ballistocardiogram parameters) can be determined).
Claims 9 and 25 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Young in view of US Patent Application Publication US-2020/0146910-A1 to Demirli et al. (hereinafter “Demirli”).
Regarding claims 9 and 25, Young discloses the system of claim 1 and the method of claim 17. Although Young discloses identifying the change in the force data greater than a predefined threshold of force, this feature does not appear to be supported by the provisional application. Further, Young does not disclose a predefined duration threshold.
However, Demirli teaches a sensor integrated into an article that is able to detect the presence of a user (change in the load on the article) based on a change in pressure data (which is force data since pressure is force applied over a given area) greater than a specified (predefined) threshold; see [0053]. Demirli further teaches that the presence of a user can be determined when the presence persists longer than a predefined (e.g.,  10 minutes) threshold period of time (duration); see [0078].
Demirli is considered to be analogous to the claimed invention because they are both within the same field of non-invasive monitoring of physiological signals using sensors attached to articles on which a user is positioned. Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified Young to incorporate the teachings of Demirli by using a predefined force threshold and a predefined duration threshold to determine the change in force data indicative of the change in the load on the article. Doing so would improve the system by allowing it to determine whether a person or object above a certain weight is on the article (see Demirli [0053]) and would provide the ability to use the duration threshold to determine that a user is in bed for the evening (see Demirli [0078]).
Claims 10 and 26 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Young in view of US Patent Application Publication US-2014/0371635-A1 to Shinar et al. (hereinafter “Shinar”).
Regarding claims 10 and 26, Young discloses the system of claim 1 and the method of claim 17 and the determination of the plurality of physiological sources on the article ([0034] states that the system can differentiate between two or more bodies (plurality of physiological sources) on the bed (article)). Young does not disclose that the determination is based on identification of alterations in the physiological signals transformed from the force data.
However, in [0110], Shinar teaches a system that determines when one person is out of bed (determination of the plurality of physiological sources on an article) by determining that the detected signals are characteristic of a second person (identification of alterations in physiological signals).
Shinar is considered to be analogous to the claimed invention because they are both within the same field of non-invasive monitoring of physiological signals using sensors attached to articles on which a user is positioned. Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified Young by incorporating the teachings of Shinar by using the physiological signals characteristic of a given user to identify when another user has left the article. Doing so would improve the system's ability to detect which user is on or off of the bed, as noted by Shinar in [0110].
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure:
US-5964720-A to Pelz;
US-8731646-B2 to Halperin et al.;
US-8905928-B2 to Hayes et al.
